title: The monstrance
hookLine: a gold sunburst that shows the host so people can pray before it
tomorrow: Could you not watch one hour (Matthew 26:40)

lines: I LOOK AT HIM. HE LOOKS AT ME.
cards: A small French village in the 1800s. The parish priest, John Vianney, kept noticing an old farmer who came into the church every day and sat for a long time in front of the tabernacle. He never seemed to move his lips.
No beads, no book. Finally the priest asked him what he said to God all that time. The farmer answered, more or less: nothing.
I look at him, and he looks at me. The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes it. And there's an object built for exactly that kind of looking.

teach.b: Monstrance comes from the Latin monstrare, to show, the same root as demonstrate. It's a holder, usually gold, with a small round window of glass in the center.

teach.h: A HOST BEHIND GLASS, A GOLD SUN.
teach.b: A single consecrated host is placed behind the glass, so people can see it. Very often, golden rays burst out around that window in every direction, like a sun.
Some are simple; some are covered in jewels and taller than a child. The host is the point; the rest is a frame. Why build such a thing?
Historians describe a medieval longing to see the host; in that period the priest began lifting it high at Mass, so everyone could look.
In 1264 the feast of Corpus Christi, the Body of Christ, was extended to the whole Church, with processions carrying the Eucharist through the streets.
People wanted to see it outside of Mass too, and the monstrance grew out of that desire. When the host is placed in a monstrance on the altar, it's called exposition.
People come and pray before it, and that's called adoration. Catholics believe they are looking at Jesus himself.
Behind it is a plain idea: prayer doesn't have to be words. You don't need to perform, or produce anything, or get it right.

teach.h: I LOOK AT HIM, AND HE LOOKS AT ME.
teach.b: You can simply sit and look, and let yourself be looked at, like the old farmer.

how: In Eucharistic adoration a priest or deacon places a consecrated host in a monstrance on the altar, and Catholics come to sit or kneel before it in silent prayer, sometimes for an hour, sometimes around the clock.

games.q: you're the priest of a French village. an old farmer sits before the tabernacle every day and never moves his lips. what do you do?
o: tell him to use a prayer book.
ask him what he says to God.
ask him to make room for others.
games.why: John Vianney asked, and the farmer said, more or less: I look at him, and he looks at me. the answer became well-known.

practice: Choose one thing near you, a candle, a tree outside the window, a cup, a photograph of someone you love, and rest your eyes on it without analyzing it or narrating it in your head.
When your mind wanders, bring your eyes back, gently. If you pray, let this looking be your prayer, with no words at all; if you don't, just practice seeing one thing fully.

wordCard.voice: Monstrance. From the Latin for showing. The gold holder, often a sunburst, that shows the host so people can pray just by looking. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: to show, to point out. It gave us monstrance and demonstrate.

carryVoice: Your line: just looking is prayer. No beads, no book, no speech required. See you tomorrow.
